Incident report: coolant pump failure at the Riverside plant.

On the morning of 14 March, a maintenance crew began a routine inspection of the secondary coolant loop. The pump had run for eleven months without a scheduled overhaul, and the vibration log showed a slow upward drift since January. The crew supervisor, who had joined the plant only two weeks earlier, asked for the bearing temperatures to be recorded before any work started. Those readings were normal. The crew then removed the inspection cover and found a thin film of oil on the coupling guard.

The oil was traced to a worn lip seal at the drive end. Replacing the seal requires removing the coupling, and removing the coupling requires lifting the motor. The crew had no lifting frame on site that day, and the work was postponed. A temporary drain was fitted, and the loop returned to service at reduced flow. The supervisor noted in the log that the seal should be replaced at the next outage.

Two days later, the vibration drift accelerated. The night operator reported a low grinding noise near the pump housing and a slight rise in motor current. He reduced the flow and informed the control room. The control room asked the day crew to inspect the coupling the next morning. However, the crew arrived to find the pump already tripped on high bearing temperature. The bearing had seized, and the shaft showed scoring along the drive end.

An investigation followed. The maintenance planner reviewed the work orders and found that the seal replacement had been scheduled twice and deferred twice, first for lack of a lifting frame and then for lack of a spare seal. The spare had been ordered, but the supplier shipped the wrong size; therefore the pump ran three more days with a leaking seal, and oil slowly escaped the coupling guard. The loss of oil starved the bearing, which then overheated and seized.

The investigation also examined why the vibration drift had not triggered a work order. The condition monitoring software calculates a moving average and raises an alert when the average exceeds a threshold. The threshold had been set during commissioning, when the pump ran at a different speed. Because the speed had been reduced the previous year, the average never crossed the threshold; however, the instantaneous vibration was well above the level seen at commissioning. The software had therefore been monitoring the wrong quantity for months; moreover, the alert routing table still listed a former engineer whose address had been retired, and any alert that did fire would have gone unanswered.

The plant has since changed three things. First, the threshold will be recalculated whenever the pump speed changes. Second, the spare seal will be held in the stores rather than ordered per job. Third, the alert routing will be tested each quarter. The supervisor has asked for a lifting frame to be kept on site, since the absence of a frame caused the first deferral. The report recommends that the same review be applied to the two other pumps on the loop, which share the seal design and the monitoring setup. A follow-up audit is due in June.

A separate review of the stores found that the spare seal had been ordered against an old part number. The number had been superseded two years earlier, and the catalogue page still showed the old size in bold type. The buyer had no way to know that the number was obsolete, because the catalogue had not been updated since the pump was installed. The report recommends that the stores list be reconciled with the current catalogue every six months, and that obsolete numbers be marked in the system so that a buyer cannot order them by accident.
